newsitem.title: USA: U.S. expands plan to slow bison killing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. expands plan to slow bison killing.

text.p: Federal officials Friday fleshed out a plan to reduce the killing of bison that roam from Yellowstone Park, saying over a third of the herd had died already this winter.

Deep snows drove the bison from the park in search of food and over 700 have been intentionally slain, as the state of Montana has insisted they be controlled to prevent the possible spread of disease to nearby cattle.

Some of the bison carry brucellosis, and the Agriculture Department's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service had threatened to revoke Montana's brucellosis-free status if the wild bison left the park for surrounding grazing lands.

Brucellosis, which has little effect on bison, causes cattle to abort calves spontaneously and to produce less milk. APHIS has conducted a costly programme over a number of years to all but eradicate the disease in U.S. cattle.
Environmentalists say there has never been a documented case of a wild bison transmitting the disease to cattle.

In a letter to Montana Gov. Marc Racicot that built on a proposal announced last week, Interior and Agriculture Department officials proposed providing additional winter range for the animals on National Forest lands and indicated new flexibility about bison and cattle co-mingling.
The officials stressed the terrible toll Arctic weather and human action have had on the bison, which until now had been the largest free-ranging herd in North America.

A recent aerial survey counted 2,145 Yellowstone bison, down from 3,436 at the start of the winter and a herd of 3,956 in early winter 1994. The officials said that the state had killed another 49 animals since the survey.

"The National Park Service believes that we are approaching population levels which may cause the population to decline below critical sustainability levels due to weather trends, and current human-caused and natural mortality," they wrote.

The agencies also proposed that if cattle and bison co-mingled, the cattle should be quarantined and checked for brucellosis, with no consequences to Montana's disease-free status if tests were negative. If the disease affected the herd, the state's status would be maintained if the herd was destroyed and no evidence of the disease cropped up in neighbouring cattle.
